text: A hallucination eval doesn't end at launch. Production traffic isn't the test set — a model that scored well in testing can still generate an unsupported claim on a question nobody thought to test.

The mechanism is a scorer — a function, often an LLM-as-judge, that runs against a call's input and output and attaches a score automatically, including a predefined scorer checking whether claims are supported by context.
Once a scorer runs, its result attaches right to that specific call — viewable alongside the input and output, not buried in a separate report.
One scored call tells you about one response. Seeing scores as columns across every call is where a pattern — one prompt template hallucinating more than others — becomes visible.
A scorer is only useful if you can isolate what it flagged. Filtering the trace table down to just the flagged calls turns a monitoring signal into an actual worklist.
Running continuously against real traffic is what a one-time eval can't do. Next up: alerting — making sure a flagged pattern actually reaches a human.
